statements.quote: Artificial intelligence has a surprisingly small cast of recurring characters.

The same names appear in the history chapters, the mathematics lessons, the interpretability labs, and the frontier surveys — sometimes as the person who proved the key theorem, sometimes as the person whose failed attempt defined the next decade's problem.
This chapter is a **who's who**: what each person contributed, why it still matters, and one or two primary sources you can read for yourself.
Every entry answers the same question in miniature — *what did this person do to AI research?* — and then points to the work where the answer is worked out.
It is deliberately not a ranking.
Credit in AI is contested, collaborative, and often late.
The person whose name is on the paper is not always the person who had the idea first, and the person who had the idea first is not always the person who made it work.
Where the record is disputed, the lesson says so.
The intellectual scaffolding predates electronic computers by a century.
These are the people who made “a machine that learns” thinkable before it was buildable.
\marginfig{ada_lovelace_portrait.jpg}{Ada Lovelace, painted by Alfred Edward Chalon.

Babbage was a mathematician and inventor who hated the errors in printed mathematical tables; that frustration drove his Difference Engine and then the Analytical Engine, a programmable machine with a store, a mill, and punched-card input.
He never saw it completed, and spent much of his fortune and the government's patience on the design.
\marginfig{charles_babbage_portrait.jpg}{Charles Babbage, 1860.
\cite{img_charles_babbage}.
Public domain.} Lovelace, the daughter of Lord Byron, was taught mathematics by Augustus De Morgan and translated Menabrea's account of the engine; her notes are longer than the original.
Note G is a step-by-step algorithm for Bernoulli numbers, traditionally described as the first published computer program.
She called her approach “poetical science” and insisted that the machine could manipulate symbols — even compose music — not merely crunch numbers.
She died at 36, and the Analytical Engine was never built (\cite[Menabrea & Lovelace, 1843]{menabrea_lovelace1843}; \cite[McCorduck, 1979]{mccorduck1979machines}).
\marginfig{alan_turing_1951.jpg}{Alan Turing, 1951.

Turing was a Cambridge mathematician who, at 24, imagined a machine with an infinite tape and a finite table of states, and used it to prove that some well-defined problems have no mechanical solution.
During the Second World War he worked at Bletchley Park on breaking the Enigma cipher, an episode that stayed secret for decades.
In 1950 he replaced “Can machines think?” with an operational question: can a machine's text responses be distinguished from a human's?
The imitation game did not settle the philosophy, but it turned a metaphysical dispute into an experiment.
He was prosecuted in 1952 for homosexuality, then a crime in Britain, and died in 1954 at 41.
His question — whether thought can be mechanized — is still the field's north star (\cite[Turing, 1936]{turing1936}; \cite[Turing, 1950]{turing1950computing}; \cite[Hodges, 1983]{hodges1983enigma}).
\marginfig{claude_shannon_portrait.jpg}{Claude Shannon.
\cite{img_claude_shannon}.
[CC BY 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/).}
Shannon was a Michigan-born mathematician and engineer whose master's thesis applied Boolean algebra to electrical relays — the idea that made digital circuit design a branch of logic.
At Bell Labs he asked what the fundamental limits of communication are, and answered with entropy and channel capacity.
He was also a playful inventor: his maze-solving mouse Theseus, his juggling, and his unicycle rides through the Bell Labs corridors were famous.
His 1951 paper framed language as a prediction problem — guess the next character, and the difficulty of the guess measures the redundancy of the text.

Every language model's training loss is a version of that measurement (\cite[Shannon, 1948]{shannon1948communication}; \cite[Shannon, 1951]{shannon1951communication}; \cite[McCorduck, 1979]{mccorduck1979machines}).

statements.quote: \marginfig{walter_pitts_1954.jpg}{Walter Pitts in 1954.

In 1943 McCulloch, a neurophysiologist, and Pitts, a self-taught logician, published **“A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity.”** They modelled the neuron as an all-or-none threshold unit and showed that networks of such units can express any function of propositional logic; with recurrent loops, the model anticipated the computational generality later formalized in automata theory.
The paper is the founding document of neural-network theory.

It gave Rosenblatt the unit he would teach, gave Hopfield the binary element his energy model would settle, and gave the field the step nonlinearity that later became the obstacle backpropagation had to overcome (\cite[McCulloch & Pitts, 1943]{mccullochpitts1943}).

Their 1947 follow-up, **“How We Know Universals,”** extended the model to the perception of auditory and visual form and anticipated the idea that nervous systems compute invariant representations (\cite[Pitts & McCulloch, 1947]{pitts1947universals}).
McCulloch collected the programme in \citetitle{mcculloch1965embodiments} (\citeyear{mcculloch1965embodiments}).
McCulloch was the group's impresario as much as its theorist.

He came to the work from philosophy, medicine and neurophysiology, moved through a series of disciplinary identities — student, poet, experimental neurologist, psychiatry resident, neurophysiologist, neuropsychiatrist, administrator, cybernetician, engineer, mentor — and treated the mind–body problem as a physiological question he called “experimental epistemology”.
His homes in Hinsdale, Old Lyme and Cambridge ran an open-door policy; students and collaborators lived there, and his mentoring was deliberately egalitarian rather than authoritarian.

The roster that passed through his circle reads like a roll-call of postwar brain science: Lettvin, Maturana, Pitts, Manuel Blum, Jack Cowan, Leo Verbeek, Bill Kilmer and Roberto Moreno-Diaz (\cite[Abraham, 2016, pp.
75–100, 153–157, 186]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).

He also wrote poetry — sonnets, mostly — and published a collection, *The Natural Fit*, in 1959; poetry was one of the identities through which he presented himself, not a hobby kept apart from the science.
At the end of his life he left an epitaph warning biographers not to sum him up, because he had always been “on an unknown way / To mine own ends”.

He died on 24 September 1969, at 70, and donated his body to Yale; Ralph Gerard's obituary called him a “rebel genius”, the phrase that became the title of Abraham's biography (\cite[Abraham, 2016, pp.
156, 186–189]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).
A McCulloch–Pitts cell: inputs are summed, compared with a threshold, and passed through an all-or-none step.
\cite{img_mcculloch_pitts_neuron}.
[CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/).
McCulloch's career reads as a sequence of identities rather than a single profession:
- **Student** — Haverford, Yale and Columbia; mathematics, philosophy, psychology and medicine.
- **Poet** — sonnets collected in *The Natural Fit* (1959).
- **Experimental neurologist** — cats, absinthe, convulsions, head injuries and cortical localisation.
- **Psychiatry assistant** — Rockland State Hospital, 1932–34, where he met Eilhard von Domarus.
- **Neurophysiologist** — Dusser de Barenne's strychnine laboratory at Yale, more than twenty papers.
- **Experimental epistemologist** — Clark Hull's seminars and a physiological theory of knowledge.
- **Theorist** — with Walter Pitts, from their meeting in 1941.
- **Mentor** — more than 120 younger collaborators and an open door.
- **Neuropsychiatrist** — the reticular formation, the chemistry of psychoses, electroconvulsive therapy.
- **Cybernetician** — chair of the Macy conferences.
- **Experimentalist** — strychnine on cortex, absinthe in cats, patients' blood in rabbits.
- **Farmer** — Old Lyme: dams, barns and a dairy herd.
- **Provocateur** — an intellectual showman who treated disciplinary boundaries as arbitrary fences.
Abraham's argument is not that these were masks over a hidden “real” McCulloch, but that the transdisciplinary life was itself the achievement (\cite[Abraham, 2016]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).
The open-door policy was literal.

In Hinsdale, Old Lyme and Cambridge, students and collaborators lived in the house; Robert Morison observed in 1947 that the household also contained the children of Stanley Gerr and Norbert Wiener's thirteen-year-old daughter, and concluded that McCulloch chose collaborators largely by how much help they needed.
His own children called their parents “Warren” and “Rook”; Jerome Lettvin remembered being listened to “as attentively as a colleague”.
Manuel Blum, who would win the Turing Award in 1995, said that McCulloch treated him as an equal when he was not one — “He really listened to what I had to say.

And I could actually read his stuff” — and that McCulloch “lifted up quite ordinary people (like me) and made them feel special.” The roster that passed through his orbit includes Lettvin, Pitts, Minsky, Papert, Maturana, Varela, Arbib, Cowan, Blum, Kauffman, Selfridge, MacKay, Kilmer, Wall, Moreno-Díaz and Verbeek.
It is the clearest evidence for McCulloch's own claim that his best work was the people he trained (\cite[Abraham, 2016]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).
Old Lyme was not a retreat from science but another site of it.
The farm McCulloch and Rook bought in 1928 became **Camp Aladdin**, a summer camp for children from Brooklyn where the children made the rules; after the Crash it became a working farm.
McCulloch calculated the hydraulics of the dam spillways himself, built a large barn in 1938 and a stone mill building in 1940, and kept a dairy herd during the Second World War.

His son David remembered that he knew which wood had which properties for which job, and that the architectural drawings always returned to symmetry — the same interest in proportion that had produced the Columbia thesis on dynamic symmetry (\cite[Abraham, 2016]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).
McCulloch's laboratory life and domestic life were equally unorthodox.
He reportedly lived on whisky and ice cream, went to bed around four in the morning, travelled in hobnailed boots, and wore a brown leather jacket under his suit jacket.

In early experiments with Elsberg and Pike he injected cats with increasing concentrations of absinthe over two hours and watched the pupils dilate, the muscles twitch, and the eyes dance with nystagmus.

With Ladislas Meduna he injected blood from schizophrenic patients into rabbits; in about 60 percent of cases the blood acted as an insulin antagonist, a result that led to the diagnosis of “oneirophrenia” (from Greek *oneiros*, dream).

None of this was mere eccentricity: the same willingness to move from poetry to hydraulics to neurochemistry is what made the transdisciplinary programme possible (\cite[Abraham, 2016]{abraham2016rebelgenius}).
Several uploads preserve the same 1969 Channel 6 Toronto interview with McCulloch; the full programme is embedded first, followed by the long excerpt and the shorter clips.
The last video is a short documentary on Walter Pitts.

Two online sources pair well with the primary literature above: the 1948 *Brooklyn Daily Eagle* clipping is reproduced with a link to the original page image \cite{afflictor2014mcculloch}, and Amanda Gefter's *Nautilus* portrait of McCulloch and Pitts is excerpted here \cite{afflictor2015mechanistic, gefter2015pitts}.
Afflictor's McCulloch tag archive collects both pieces in one place \cite{afflictor_mcculloch_tag}.
An IBM 704 at NASA Langley, 1957 — the machine on which Samuel's later checkers program ran.
The connectionist line was not the only one to leave the laboratory.
In the 1970s a second group decided that the bottleneck was not the learning rule but **knowledge** itself, and built systems that encoded a specialist's rules explicitly.

**Edward Feigenbaum** and **Bruce Buchanan** at Stanford turned that conviction into DENDRAL, which inferred molecular structures from mass spectra, and then MYCIN, which diagnosed blood infections from a few hundred IF–THEN rules.

MYCIN separated its rule base from its inference engine, so the engine could be reused as the first expert-system shell, EMYCIN, and in a blind clinical test it prescribed antibiotics as well as, or better than, nine human clinicians \cite{crevier1993ai}.

Feigenbaum called the activity **knowledge engineering**, and it became the commercial face of AI in the 1980s (\cite[Feigenbaum, 1984]{feigenbaum1984expert}; \cite[Shortliffe & Buchanan, 1976]{shortliffe1976mycin}).

**John McDermott**'s XCON (originally R1) took the recipe to the Digital Equipment Corporation, where it configured VAX machines and grew from about three hundred rules in 1979 to more than three thousand by 1984 \cite{crevier1993ai}.

**Douglas Lenat** pushed the same bet further: his AM and Eurisko programs tried to discover mathematical concepts and new heuristics, and when that programme stalled he began **Cyc**, a hand-built common-sense ontology measured in person-centuries of knowledge engineering (\cite[Cyc]{cyc_wiki}; \cite{crevier1993ai}).
The lesson of this generation is the one the neural revival would later overturn: intelligence was supposed to live in the rules, and the rules had to be written by hand.
\marginfig{john_hopfield_portrait.jpg}{John Hopfield.
\cite{img_john_hopfield}.
[CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/).}
Hopfield trained as a physicist, worked at Bell Labs and Princeton, and came to neural networks from the physics of collective behaviour.
His 1982 paper treated the network as an energy landscape: stored patterns are minima, and recall is relaxation downhill.
The model made associative memory rigorous, connected neural networks to statistical physics, and helped restart a field that had been in retreat since the perceptron critique.
He shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics with Geoffrey Hinton for these foundations (\cite[Hopfield, 1982]{hopfield1982}; \cite[Nobel Prize, 2024]{nobel2024physics}).

statements.quote: \marginfig{paul_werbos_portrait.jpg}{Paul Werbos at IJCNN Seattle, 1991.
Werbos published the first derivation of backpropagation for neural networks in his 1974 Harvard dissertation, **Beyond Regression**, more than a decade before the 1986 paper made it famous.

He also developed **backpropagation through time** for recurrent networks and the **adaptive critic** family of designs — a learned value model guiding a learned policy — which he later called approximate dynamic programming.
His experience is the field's standard cautionary tale about how long a good idea can sit unread (\cite[Werbos, 1974]{werbos1974}; \cite[Werbos, 1990]{werbos1990bptt}).
\marginfig{yann_lecun_portrait.jpg}{Yann LeCun.
[CC BY-SA 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/).}
LeCun grew up in France, studied in Paris, and joined Bell Labs, where he combined convolutional weight-sharing with backpropagation to recognize handwritten ZIP codes for the U.S.
Postal Service in 1989; the later LeNet-5 was deployed in bank check-reading systems.
He later founded NYU's CILVR lab and Meta's FAIR, and has spent the last decade arguing that self-supervised world models, not next-token prediction alone, are the path to general intelligence.
He shared the 2018 Turing Award with Hinton and Bengio (\cite[LeCun et al., 1989]{lecun1989backpropagation}; \cite[LeCun, 2022]{lecun2022path}).
\marginfig{yoshua_bengio_portrait.jpg}{Yoshua Bengio.
\cite{img_yoshua_bengio}.
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).}
Bengio grew up in France and Canada, trained as a computer scientist, and built Mila in Montreal into one of the world's leading academic deep-learning labs.
His 2003 neural probabilistic language model replaced sparse n-gram tables with dense, learned word embeddings — the direct ancestor of the input layer of every modern language model.

He shared the 2018 Turing Award with Hinton and LeCun, and has become one of the most prominent scientific voices on AI safety, arguing that the field needs international coordination and a precautionary approach (\cite[Bengio et al., 2003]{neuralprobabilistic}; \cite[Bengio et al., 2023]{bengio2023managing}).
\marginfig{sepp_hochreiter_portrait.jpg}{Sepp Hochreiter at his institute, 2015.
\cite{img_sepp_hochreiter}.
Their 1997 **Long Short-Term Memory** introduced the cell state and the gating mechanism that let recurrent networks carry information across many steps without the vanishing gradient destroying it.
LSTM dominated sequence modelling for two decades — speech, translation, handwriting, time series — and its gated-residual idea is still visible in modern architectures.
\marginfig{juergen_schmidhuber_portrait.jpg}{Jürgen Schmidhuber at the AI for Good summit, 2017.
\cite{img_juergen_schmidhuber}.

[CC BY 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/).} The Transformer replaced the recurrence, not the lesson: a network needs a protected path for information to survive depth and time (\cite[Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997]{lstm}).
AlexNet, split across two GPUs: five convolutional layers, three fully connected layers, and a 1000-way softmax.

statements.quote: \marginfig{david_silver_portrait.jpg}{David Silver.
Silver studied at Cambridge and UCL, joined DeepMind in 2010, and led the AlphaGo team that combined deep policy and value networks with Monte Carlo tree search to beat Lee Sedol in 2016.
He then led AlphaZero, which learned chess, shogi, and Go from the rules alone by self-play (\cite[Silver et al., 2016]{silver2016alphago}; \cite[Silver et al., 2018]{silver2018zero}).
MuZero carried the idea further, learning a model of the environment's dynamics and planning inside it without being given the rules (\cite[Schrittwieser et al., 2020]{schrittwieser2020muzero}).
\marginfig{demis_hassabis_portrait.jpg}{Demis Hassabis.
\cite{img_demis_hassabis}.

[CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).} Hassabis co-founded DeepMind after a career that included neuroscience research at UCL — including work on how patients with hippocampal amnesia imagine new experiences (\cite[Hassabis et al., 2007]{hassabis2007patients}) — and built the organization that made both projects possible; he shared one half of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with John Jumper for AlphaFold, while David Baker received the other half for computational protein design (\cite[Jumper et al., 2021]{jumper2021alphafold}; \cite[Nobel Prize, 2024]{nobel2024chemistry}; \cite[DeepMind, 2024]{deepmind_about}).
Silver and Sutton's later essay argues that reward maximization is sufficient for intelligence in general, not just for games (\cite[Silver et al., 2021]{silver2021reward}).
\marginfig{john_jumper_portrait.jpg}{John Jumper.
Jumper is a computational chemist who joined DeepMind in 2017 and led the AlphaFold team.
He had worked on protein folding as a student and knew the problem's reputation: a protein's function is determined by its three-dimensional shape, but the space of possible folds is astronomical.

AlphaFold 2's accuracy at CASP14 in 2020 turned a decades-old grand challenge into a practical tool, and AlphaFold 3 extended the approach to biomolecular complexes (\cite[Jumper et al., 2021]{jumper2021alphafold}; \cite[Abramson et al., 2024]{alphafold3}).
He shared one half of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Hassabis; David Baker received the other half (\cite[Nobel Prize, 2024]{nobel2024chemistry}; \cite[DeepMind, 2024]{deepmind_about}).
\marginfig{richard_sutton_portrait.jpg}{Richard Sutton.
\cite{img_richard_sutton}.
Sutton grew up in Canada, did a PhD at UMass Amherst, and worked at AT&T Bell Labs before returning to Alberta; Barto was his UMass colleague and coauthor.
Together they built temporal-difference learning, the value-function view, and the textbook that trained the field.

Sutton's “The Bitter Lesson” is the clearest statement of the scaling worldview — general methods that exploit computation beat methods with built-in human knowledge — and it remains the most cited argument for the approach that produced modern LLMs.
In 2024 they shared the ACM Turing Award (\cite[Sutton, 1988]{sutton1988td}; \citetitle{sutton2018rlbook}; \cite[Sutton, 2019]{sutton2019bitter}; \cite[ACM, 2024]{acm2024turing}).
Two attention heads from layer 5 of 6 in the original Transformer, tracking how the word “its” resolves to different antecedents in different contexts.
\cite{img_transformer_attention_heads}.
[CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).
The people below built the formal and institutional foundations on which everything else rests.
Their work is older than the label “AI,” but the field's central questions — what can be computed, what can be represented, and what can be learned — are theirs.
\marginfig{george_boole_portrait.jpg}{George Boole.
\marginfig{gottlob_frege_portrait.jpg}{Gottlob Frege.
\cite{img_gottlob_frege}.
Boole's **Laws of Thought** (1854) turned Aristotle's syllogisms into algebra: propositions become variables, “and” and “or” become operations, and logical inference becomes calculation.
Every digital circuit and every symbolic AI system is downstream of that move (\citetitle{boole1854}).

Frege's **Begriffsschrift** (1879) went further, inventing predicate logic and the quantifier notation that made it possible to express statements about *all* or *some* objects — the logical grammar that Russell and Whitehead later built into *Principia Mathematica* (\citetitle{frege1879}).

Church's lambda calculus gave computation a second formal language, and his 1936 proof that the Entscheidungsproblem is unsolvable established that not every well-defined mathematical question has a mechanical answer (\cite[Church, 1936]{church1936}).

Turing's contemporaneous paper on computable numbers introduced the abstract machine that now bears his name, proved the same negative result by a different route, and gave the field its standard model of what a computer *is* (\citetitle{turing1936}).
The Church–Turing thesis — that every effectively calculable function is computable by a Turing machine — is the unspoken premise of every neural network.
\marginfig{john_mccarthy_portrait.jpg}{John McCarthy.

statements.section: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon

statements.quote: The 1955 **Dartmouth proposal** named the field and set its first research agenda: language, neurons, abstraction, and creativity, all to be studied by building machines that could exhibit them (\cite[McCarthy et al., 1955]{mccarthy1955dartmouth}).
statements.section: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon

statements.quote: McCarthy went on to invent LISP and to argue that common-sense knowledge could be represented as explicit logical statements — the symbolic programme that dominated AI's first decades.
statements.section: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon

statements.quote: Minsky co-founded MIT's AI laboratory and later wrote *The Society of Mind*, a book-length argument that intelligence is a society of simpler agents rather than a single monolithic algorithm.
statements.section: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon

statements.quote: \marginfig{simon_newell.jpg}{Herbert A.
\cite{simonnewell_image}.
Simon and Newell built the **Logic Theory Machine**, one of the first programs to prove theorems, and used it to argue that human problem solving is symbol manipulation.

The program proved 38 of the first 52 theorems in *Principia Mathematica* and found a shorter proof of theorem 2.85 than Russell and Whitehead's; when the authors submitted that proof to the *Journal of Symbolic Logic* with the program listed as a co-author, the editor rejected it because proving a theorem in the outmoded system of *Principia* was no accomplishment \cite{crevier1993ai}.
Their **physical symbol system hypothesis** — that a physical symbol system has the necessary and sufficient means for general intelligent action — became the philosophical core of classical AI.

Simon also won the Nobel Prize in Economics for his work on bounded rationality, a reminder that the study of intelligence has always crossed disciplinary lines (\cite[Newell & Simon, 1956]{newell1956logic}).

Ashby's **Design for a Brain** defined adaptation as the maintenance of essential variables within viable limits and built the **Homeostat**, a machine that reorganized its own connections until it recovered stability.
statements.section: W. Ross Ashby and Donald Hebb

statements.quote: His “law of requisite variety” — only variety can absorb variety — is still the best one-line statement of why control requires internal complexity (\citetitle{ashbydesigndbrain1952}).
statements.section: W. Ross Ashby and Donald Hebb

statements.quote: Hebb's **The Organization of Behavior** proposed that repeated co-activation strengthens synapses, the rule that Rosenblatt turned into the perceptron's error-correction mechanism (\citetitle{hebb1949organizationofbehaviour}).
statements.section: W. Ross Ashby and Donald Hebb

statements.quote: He's **ResNet** introduced the residual connection — learn a *delta* rather than a full transformation — and made networks with hundreds of layers trainable.
The idea is so basic that it now appears in almost every deep architecture, including the Transformer's own residual stream (\cite[He et al., 2016]{he2016resnet}).
Dosovitskiy's **Vision Transformer** treated an image as a sequence of patches and showed that a plain Transformer, with enough data, could match or beat convolutional networks.
That result opened the path to the unified multimodal models of the 2020s (\cite[Dosovitskiy et al., 2020]{dosovitskiy2020vit}).

The **U-Net** paired a contracting encoder with an expanding decoder and skip connections, giving image generation and segmentation a precise spatial backbone; it is still the default architecture inside diffusion models (\cite[Ronneberger et al., 2015]{ronneberger2015unet}).

**pix2pix** showed that a conditional GAN could learn image-to-image translation from paired examples — edges to photographs, maps to aerial views, day to night — and made “image translation” a standard task (\cite[Isola et al., 2017]{isola2017pix2pix}).
Ho's **DDPM** made diffusion models practical by learning to reverse a fixed noising process one small step at a time (\cite[Ho et al., 2020]{ho2020ddpm}).
statements.section: Jonathan Ho, Yang Song, and Robin Rombach

statements.quote: Song's score-based formulation provided the continuous-time view — learn the gradient of the log density, then follow it back to data — that unified diffusion with earlier energy-based methods (\cite[Song & Ermon, 2019]{song2019score}).
statements.section: Jonathan Ho, Yang Song, and Robin Rombach

statements.quote: Rombach's **latent diffusion** moved the whole process into a compressed image space, cutting the compute enough to put Stable Diffusion on a consumer GPU (\cite[Rombach et al., 2022]{rombach2022ldm}).
statements.section: Jonathan Ho, Yang Song, and Robin Rombach

statements.quote: Ramesh's **DALL·E** was an autoregressive Transformer over discrete image tokens — a direct application of the language-model recipe to pixels (\cite[Ramesh et al., 2021]{ramesh2021dalle}).
statements.section: Aditya Ramesh, Alec Radford, and William Peebles

statements.quote: Radford's **CLIP** learned a shared image-text space from hundreds of millions of pairs by contrastive training, giving text-to-image systems a semantic steering wheel (\cite[Radford et al., 2021]{radford2021clip}); his GPT-2 and Whisper work did the same for open-ended text and speech (\cite[Radford et al., 2019]{radford2019language}; \cite[Radford et al., 2022]{radford2022whisper}).
statements.section: Aditya Ramesh, Alec Radford, and William Peebles

statements.quote: Peebles' **Diffusion Transformer** replaced the U-Net with a plain Transformer over latent patches and became the backbone of Sora, FLUX, and Stable Diffusion 3 (\cite[Peebles & Xie, 2023]{peebles2023dit}).
statements.section: Aditya Ramesh, Alec Radford, and William Peebles

statements.quote: The language-model stack was assembled from many small inventions.
These are the people whose papers supply the pieces.
\marginfig{tomas_mikolov_portrait.jpg}{Tomáš Mikolov.
\cite{img_tomas_mikolov}.

Mikolov's **word2vec** trained dense word vectors on local context windows and showed that their differences encode analogies — “king − man + woman ≈ queen” (\cite[Mikolov et al., 2013]{mikolov2013word2vec}).

Pennington's **GloVe** reached the same geometry from the opposite direction, factorizing the global co-occurrence matrix so that dot products approximate log counts (\cite[Pennington et al., 2014]{pennington2014glove}).
Together they made the embedding layer a standard component of neural language models.

Sennrich's **subword BPE** solved the out-of-vocabulary problem by learning a vocabulary of frequent character fragments, so any word can be reconstructed from pieces (\cite[Sennrich et al., 2016]{sennrich2016subword}).

Kudo's **SentencePiece** made the same idea language-independent by treating whitespace as a normal symbol, which is why multilingual models can tokenize Chinese, English, and code with one vocabulary (\cite[Kudo & Richardson, 2018]{kudo2018sentencepiece}).

Devlin's **BERT** trained a bidirectional encoder with masked language modelling and established the pretrain-then-fine-tune paradigm for understanding tasks (\cite[Devlin et al., 2019]{devlin2019bert}).
statements.section: Jacob Devlin, Yinhan Liu, and Colin Raffel

statements.quote: Liu's **RoBERTa** showed that BERT was undertrained: remove next-sentence prediction, resample masks dynamically, train longer on more data, and the same architecture sets new records (\cite[Liu et al., 2019]{liu2019roberta}).
statements.section: Jacob Devlin, Yinhan Liu, and Colin Raffel

statements.quote: Raffel's **T5** unified translation, summarization, classification, and question answering into one text-to-text format with span-corruption pretraining (\cite[Raffel et al., 2020]{raffel2020t5}).
statements.section: Jacob Devlin, Yinhan Liu, and Colin Raffel

statements.quote: A frontier model is not just an algorithm; it is a distributed system.
These people made the difference between a paper and a training run.
\marginfig{jeff_dean_portrait.jpg}{Jeff Dean.
statements.section: Jeff Dean, Samyam Rajbhandari, and Dmitry Lepikhin

statements.quote: Dean's **DistBelief** showed that neural networks could be trained across thousands of machines, and his later work on TensorFlow and TPUs made that infrastructure usable (\cite[Dean et al., 2012]{dean2012large}).
statements.section: Jeff Dean, Samyam Rajbhandari, and Dmitry Lepikhin

statements.quote: Rajbhandari's **ZeRO** partitioned optimizer states, gradients, and parameters across data-parallel workers, removing the memory duplication that had blocked trillion-parameter training (\cite[Rajbhandari et al., 2020]{rajbhandari2020zero}).
statements.section: Jeff Dean, Samyam Rajbhandari, and Dmitry Lepikhin

statements.quote: Lepikhin's **GShard** combined mixture-of-experts routing with automatic sharding, making sparse models practical at scale (\cite[Lepikhin et al., 2021]{lepikhin2021gshard}).
statements.section: Jeff Dean, Samyam Rajbhandari, and Dmitry Lepikhin

statements.quote: Fedus's **Switch Transformer** simplified MoE routing to one expert per token and scaled it to trillion-parameter models (\cite[Fedus et al., 2022]{fedus2022switch}).
statements.section: William Fedus, Tri Dao, and Woosuk Kwon

statements.quote: Dao's **FlashAttention** made exact attention IO-aware: it tiles the computation to fit in GPU on-chip memory instead of materializing the full attention matrix (\cite[Dao et al., 2022]{dao2022flashattention}).
statements.section: William Fedus, Tri Dao, and Woosuk Kwon

statements.quote: Kwon's **vLLM** introduced PagedAttention, managing the KV cache in fixed-size blocks like an operating system's virtual memory; it turned serving from a memory-fragmentation problem into a throughput problem (\cite[Kwon et al., 2023]{kwon2023vllm}).
statements.section: William Fedus, Tri Dao, and Woosuk Kwon

statements.quote: Olah's **circuits thread** reframed neural networks as objects to be reverse-engineered: features are directions, circuits are subgraphs, and the goal is a mechanistic explanation of behavior (\cite[Olah et al., 2020]{olaha2020zoomin}).
statements.section: Chris Olah, Nelson Elhage, and Trenton Bricken

statements.quote: Elhage's **Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits** formalized the residual stream and the QK/OV circuits, and his **Toy Models of Superposition** explained why neurons are polysemantic: networks pack more features than dimensions by using nearly orthogonal directions (\cite[Elhage et al., 2021]{elhage2021mathematical}; \cite[Elhage et al., 2022]{elhage2022superposition}).
statements.section: Chris Olah, Nelson Elhage, and Trenton Bricken

statements.quote: Bricken's **Towards Monosemanticity** showed that sparse autoencoders could recover interpretable features from superposition, the technique later scaled to production models (\cite[Bricken et al., 2023]{bricken2023monosemanticity}).
statements.section: Chris Olah, Nelson Elhage, and Trenton Bricken

statements.quote: Zou's **representation engineering** turned interpretability into a top-down toolkit for reading and controlling high-level properties such as honesty and power-seeking (\cite[Zou et al., 2023]{zou2023repeng}).
statements.section: Andy Zou and Alexander Matt Turner

statements.quote: Turner's **activation addition** showed that a single contrastive direction — “Love” minus “Hate” — could steer a model's sentiment at inference time without any training (\cite[Turner et al., 2023]{turner2023actadd}).
statements.section: Andy Zou and Alexander Matt Turner

statements.quote: \marginfig{dario_amodei_portrait.jpg}{Dario Amodei.
statements.section: Collin Burns, Dario Amodei, and Geoffrey Irving

statements.quote: Burns' **weak-to-strong generalization** fine-tuned strong models on labels from weak supervisors to measure how much latent capability could be elicited — a present-day proxy for the alignment problem (\cite[Burns et al., 2023]{burns2023weakstrong}).
statements.section: Collin Burns, Dario Amodei, and Geoffrey Irving

statements.quote: Amodei's **Concrete Problems in AI Safety** named the failure modes that the field still uses as its taxonomy: reward hacking, side effects, scalable oversight, safe exploration, and distributional shift (\cite[Amodei et al., 2016]{amodei2016concrete}).
statements.section: Collin Burns, Dario Amodei, and Geoffrey Irving

statements.quote: Irving's **AI safety via debate** proposed training two models to argue opposite sides of a question in front of a human judge, so that the judge can supervise answers too complex to verify directly (\cite[Irving et al., 2018]{irving2018debate}).
statements.section: Collin Burns, Dario Amodei, and Geoffrey Irving

statements.quote: Russell's **Human Compatible** argues that the standard objective-based model of AI is the problem: a machine optimizing a fixed objective will resist correction, so the design goal should be uncertainty about human preferences and a willingness to be switched off (\citetitle{russell2019human}).
statements.section: Stuart Russell, Nick Bostrom, Eliezer Yudkowsky, and Toby Ord

statements.quote: Bostrom's **Superintelligence** framed the control problem and the orthogonality thesis — intelligence and final goals are independent — for a broad audience (\citetitle{bostrom2014superintelligence}).
statements.section: Stuart Russell, Nick Bostrom, Eliezer Yudkowsky, and Toby Ord

statements.quote: Yudkowsky's earlier essay on AI as a global risk factor made the case that a sufficiently capable optimizer need not be malevolent to be dangerous (\cite[Yudkowsky, 2008]{yudkowsky2008ai}).
statements.section: Stuart Russell, Nick Bostrom, Eliezer Yudkowsky, and Toby Ord

statements.quote: Ord's **The Precipice** places AI risk alongside pandemics and nuclear war in a broader ethics of existential risk (\citetitle{ord2020precipice}).

statements.quote: Tesauro's **TD-Gammon** combined self-play with temporal-difference learning and a neural network, reaching master-level backgammon and demonstrating that value learning from self-generated experience could work at scale (\cite[Tesauro, 1995]{tesauro1995tdgammon}).
statements.section: Gerald Tesauro, Volodymyr Mnih, and John Schulman

statements.quote: Mnih's **DQN** learned Atari games directly from pixels with a convolutional network and experience replay, the result that launched deep reinforcement learning (\cite[Mnih et al., 2015]{mnih2015dqn}).
statements.section: Gerald Tesauro, Volodymyr Mnih, and John Schulman

statements.quote: Schulman's **PPO** made policy-gradient training stable enough to become the default algorithm for RLHF and for many game-playing systems (\cite[Schulman et al., 2017]{schulman2017ppo}).
statements.section: Gerald Tesauro, Volodymyr Mnih, and John Schulman

statements.quote: Shao's **DeepSeekMath** introduced **GRPO**, the group-relative policy optimization that removes the critic by normalizing rewards across sampled answers to the same prompt.
GRPO made verifiable-reward RL cheap enough to run at scale and became the optimization engine behind DeepSeek-R1 and many open reasoning models (\cite[Shao et al., 2024]{shao2024grpo}).

The history of AI is not a list of lone geniuses.
Ideas arrive in clusters, are independently discovered, and are often named after the person who made them famous rather than the person who had them first.
Backpropagation is the canonical example: Werbos derived it in 1974, Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams made it famous in 1986, and Linnainmaa had described the reverse-mode chain rule earlier still.
The perceptron has its own priority dispute: Farley and Clark built a perceptron-like device before Rosenblatt, but did not build the theory around it.
The Transformer had eight authors, and its key ideas drew on attention mechanisms developed for translation.
This chapter names people because names are how the course's citations, biographies, and Atlas entries are organized — not because the field's progress can be reduced to a list of individuals.
The primary sources are the point.
